stem: Which factors are used to calculate a kidney candidate's Estimated Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) score per standard waitlist references?

options.text: Time on dialysis, diabetes status, prior solid-organ transplant, and candidate age
Donor creatinine and donor hypertension history only
Recipient blood type without any clinical variables

explanation.rationale_correct: The EPTS score is based on the candidate's time on dialysis, whether the candidate has diabetes, whether the candidate received any prior solid-organ transplant, and the candidate's age.

rationale_incorrect.B: Donor creatinine and hypertension contribute to KDPI rather than EPTS.
rationale_incorrect.C: PRA reflects sensitization but is not the EPTS calculation basis.
rationale_incorrect.D: EPTS incorporates clinical survival predictors rather than blood type alone.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: EPTS score is based on all of the following: Candidate's time on dialysis … diagnosis of diabetes … prior SOT … candidate's age

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → Kidney transplantation → EPTS → b.ii. (dialysis time, diabetes, prior SOT, age); PDF p. 49 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. First EPTS item in bank; distinct from inactive waiting-time rules (cctc-2037) and KDPI mention in batch-01; anchor verified on Cupples p. 49.

stem: When presenting deceased-donor kidney quality to the team, which donor characteristics contribute to the Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) per standard references?

options.text: Donor age, creatinine, hypertension and diabetes history, cause of death, and HCV status among other factors
Number of post-transplant clinic visits only

explanation.rationale_correct: KDPI is derived from the Kidney Donor Risk Index using donor characteristics including age, ethnicity, creatinine, hypertension, diabetes, cause of death, height, weight, DCD status, and HCV status.

rationale_incorrect.B: Recipient dialysis time contributes to EPTS rather than KDPI.
rationale_incorrect.C: EBV serostatus guides infection prophylaxis rather than KDPI calculation.
rationale_incorrect.D: KDPI reflects donor quality metrics rather than post-transplant visit counts.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: KDPI score is derived from the Kidney Donor Risk Index … Age … Creatinine … hypertension … diabetes … Cause of death … HCV status

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → Kidney transplantation → KDPI → c.ii. (donor age, creatinine, comorbidities, DCD, HCV, etc.); PDF p. 49 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. KDPI donor-factor angle distinct from EPTS candidate score (cctc-2097) and DonorNet offer presentation (cctc-2016); anchor verified on Cupples p. 49.

stem: During heart transplant evaluation, the team reviews a candidate's smoking history. Which post-transplant risk should the coordinator include in counseling per standard references?

options.text: Increased risk of coronary atherosclerosis, graft dysfunction, and graft loss
Complete elimination of coronary artery disease risk after transplant
Smoking history is irrelevant once the candidate is listed
Smoking protects against chronic rejection in heart recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Heart transplant recipients with a smoking history have increased risk of developing coronary atherosclerosis, graft dysfunction, and loss after transplantation.

rationale_incorrect.B: Smoking history increases cardiovascular and graft risks rather than eliminating coronary disease.
rationale_incorrect.C: Smoking history remains relevant to long-term heart graft outcomes after listing.
rationale_incorrect.D: Smoking is associated with worse graft outcomes rather than rejection protection.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: Heart transplant recipients with a smoking history have an increased risk of developing coronary atherosclerosis, graft dysfunction, and loss

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → Pulmonary evaluation → 2.e.i. (heart smoking risks: coronary atherosclerosis, graft dysfunction/loss); PDF p. 33 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Heart-smoking counseling angle distinct from kidney smoking risks (cctc-1098) and liver smoking complications (cctc-2095); anchor verified on Cupples p. 33.

stem: A kidney candidate has a willing, medically suitable living donor who is incompatible with the intended recipient. Which transplant option should the coordinator discuss per standard references?

options.text: Kidney paired donation through the OPTN KPD program
Permanent exclusion from all transplantation because the donor is incompatible
Immediate deceased-donor-only listing with no living-donor alternatives
Kidney paired donation is available only outside the United States

explanation.rationale_correct: Kidney paired donation is a potential option for candidates with a willing, medically suitable living donor who is incompatible with the intended recipient; in the United States the KPD program is part of the OPTN.

rationale_incorrect.B: Incompatible living donation may be addressed through paired exchange rather than permanent exclusion.
rationale_incorrect.C: KPD is a living-donor pathway when direct donation is incompatible.
rationale_incorrect.D: The United States KPD Pilot Program is part of the OPTN rather than being unavailable domestically.
